c_clownbill.text: It's a puffin. It has seen the cliffs, the sea and you, and has decided you are the least interesting.

c_plungebeak.text: A gannet dive-bombs a shoal below the cliff and comes up looking smug.

c_billgruff.text: Burren goats have lived wild on the limestone since the Bronze Age. This one wants your sandwich. This one is not going to ask nicely.

c_kidgruff.text: A kid goat bounces off the boulder, lands neatly on the next one, and refuses to say how.

c_gentlet.text: A deep blue spring gentian, one of the bluest things in nature. It's about the size of your thumbnail and entirely unbothered.

burren_botanist.text: Of Ireland's twenty-eight native orchid species, twenty-four grow on the Burren, give or take. I count them in the rain.
Spring gentian, mountain avens, bloody cranesbill. They're all up at once in May. It's like a traffic jam of confetti.

dolmen_guide.text: This is Poulnabrone. Two portal stones, a thin slab on top and a lot of questions. About 3800 BC. It's older than the pyramids at Giza, which is a lovely thing to say to an Egyptian.
It's a tomb, not an altar. No sacrifices. Just ancestors and a rather excellent view.

cliff_guide.text: The Cliffs of Moher go up two hundred and fourteen metres at the highest, and the sea at the bottom always looks like it's a long way off. It is.
Don't climb the wall. I've seen what the wind does to hats, and I've seen hats do things to people.

cheese_farmer.text: Burren farmers winter their cattle on the hills, not in the valleys, so the limestone stays warm. It's called winterage. It's thousands of years old.
The cattle graze the flowers, which keeps the rare ones from being swamped. It's the one place where a cow is a conservationist.

cave_guide.text: Under the Burren there are miles of caves. In Doolin there's a stalactite that's over seven metres long, hanging from the ceiling like a very slow icicle.
I do the tours. You wear a helmet. If you hear dripping, it's not a leak. It's a million years of progress.

landsky_burren_karst.text: {greeting} I'm chasing a river. It went underground about a mile back and I'd like to know where it comes out. That's the Burren for you: the water has its own ideas.

It's karst, the word's from Slovenia. Rain picks up a bit of carbon dioxide and eats limestone, so streams sink, caves open, and the lakes come and go. A turlough fills from below in winter and drains in summer, and the cattle graze where the fish were.

The rock was a warm sea floor 330 million years ago, when Ireland sat near the equator. Ice scraped it bare, rain carved it, and the grykes keep gentians and orchids warm. There's a thousand years of rain in every crack, and it's still coming down. Ah, there's my river, listen. Under your feet.
